messages.subject: Design issue point count sampling
parts:
Hi all,
I am quite new in Distance, using Distance for Windows. 
I want to analyse bird data from three consecutive years - 2020, 2021, 2022 with two visits each year, in total 6 for all forest fragments with 74 randomly selected point plots (5 %). My survey covers 16 forest fragments ranging in size, and with total area of 3413 ha and 63 registered species. I have > 50 observations for 20 of the registered species. 
I find it difficult to organise my data and derive density and abundance estimates as follows:
1. For each species in the different forest fragments;
2. Each species for the total survey area (16 forests);
3. And annual estimes for the whole area for all species (or I should use only those with enough observations?).

I am attaching screenshots for (1) example of species design and (2) all species with stratum "year". Another question is the survey effort - should it be from 1 to 6 for each visit? 
I can see that my first attempt with the individual species was wrong (1), as I am missing the point stations without observation of the species, thus my estimates were inflated. 
Any advice will be very helpful.
Thank you very much in advance!
Kind regards,
Polina

messages.subject: Re: {Suspected Spam} [distance-sampling] Design issue point count sampling
parts:
Polina

That is quite an ambitious survey. The question about how to organise your data is tied to the design of your survey and the estimates you wish (robustly) produce. Your email covers survey design, data organisation and (tacitly) modelling strategy. Our discussion may take a few iterations to arrive at a solution.

I understand that in a perfect situation, you would like to produce estimates for each (let's say 20) species in each of 16 forest fragments in each of three years. That would amount to 960 estimates. I suspect that is beyond the reach of your data unless you make (untestable) assumptions about detectability; i.e. detectability is the same across some combination of years/fragments/species. Using pooled detection function to produce estimates at lower levels of data organisation is likely to produce biased estimates. In your situation, if you pool data across fragments for fitting detection functions, then try to produce fragment-specific estimates, those estimates are likely to be biased. This is discussed in this paper
  • Rexstad, E., Buckland, S., Marshall, L., & Borchers, D. (2023). Pooling robustness in distance sampling: Avoiding bias when there is unmodelled heterogeneity. Ecology and Evolution, 13(1), e9684. https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.9684

From the survey design information you provided, there are 74 point transects spread across 16 fragments; resulting in an average of 4.6 points per fragment. That is a low level of replication for fragment-specific estimates; we recommend a level of replication closer to 15-20 transects per stratum. Is there some natural combining of adjacent fragments (giving rise to new geographic strata) that would be sensible for producing meaningful estimates with an increased number of spatial replicate points? For example, if it makes sense to merge 4 nearby fragments into a single stratum, you would increase the number of transects to ~18. There may also be beneficial effects of increasing number of detections per stratum. The answer to this question will have consequences for your data entry.

For the first two types of estimates you want (species within fragments, species over entire study area) you make no mention of how you intend to treat year. Assuming you want year-specificity in this, you could consider merging year and fragment into strata (Begovo20, Begovo21, Begovo22, etc; similar to what you have in your second screenshot).

Your comments in your last paragraph:
  • if you visited each point twice during the year, then Effort would be recorded as 2. It is sensible to pool detections across visits within year.
  • you are right, creating projects specific to each species is probably a bad idea for two reasons
    • it is more work to duplication the design information in each project (you can use the data filter to subset the entire dataset for separate species)
    • as you noted, if species are not detected at some points, effort can be misrepresented producing positive bias in your estimates.

As you can see, there are many issues embedded in your email. One step you have already begun (you noted the number of species for which you have >50 detections) is to summarise your data before entering them into Distance for Windows. In your spreadsheet, you could produce tabulations of the number of detections by species, year, fragment (perhaps with various spatial definitions of fragments—see my earlier comment regarding this). This will inform your decisions regarding the amount of support your detection function models might have, having consequences for the strength of your inferences.

Now you can see the likely iterative nature of this conversation. There is likely compromise to be made between the level of inference you wish to make (960 independent estimates) and the support for that degree of inference in your data. If you want to continue this dialogue, we could carry on off-list and you could come back to the list with final conclusions.
